Tuesday night
Something's not right with Parveen. This week she gave me her favourite bracelet and her whole shelf of novels. She said, "I won't need them." She's stopped coming to lunch. It's so hot and she keeps wearing full sleeves. Some girls in class were whispering about her, and I told them to stop.
At break I found her alone by the water tank. I said, "I've noticed you're not yourself. I'm worried about you." She said, "I'm just tired of everything. Nothing's going to get better."
I didn't leave her. I said, "Come with me," and we went to Ms Fernandes, the counsellor, right then. Ms Fernandes kept her there and called her mother, who came to school before the last bell.
Vinita

passage: I'm Minakshi, Bidisha's mother. I found out in March, when I saw a bandage she hadn't mentioned and then the marks under it. My first reaction was panic. I wanted to scream, to ask what I had done wrong, to lock away everything in the house. I was so angry, but mostly at myself. I went into the bathroom and breathed for two minutes. Then I sat on her bed and said, "I'm not angry with you. I'm here, and we'll get help together." She cried and cried. I didn't leave her that night. We called the helpline, and the next morning I took her to our doctor, who referred us to a psychologist. If I'd punished her, I think I'd have lost her trust. Instead, she talks to me now.

passage: I'm Deepak, and I've taught maths for twelve years. What I remember most is a Tuesday in October. Nitin, a quiet boy in Class 10, stayed after class and said, "Sir, I don't think I'm okay. I can't stop feeling scared." I wanted to say, "It's just board exam stress, everyone feels it." I stopped myself. I put down my chalk, sat on the bench beside him and said, "Thank you for telling me. That took courage." I listened without lecturing. Then I said, "Let's go to the counsellor now, together." She saw him that period, and with his agreement, called his parents. Months later, Nitin told me he'd almost not come to me. If I'd brushed him off, he'd never have asked anyone again.

qa.a: Nitin might have felt ashamed and alone and never asked anyone for help again.

passage: Jagdish, twenty, helped on the family farm by day and studied for his correspondence degree at night. For six weeks now, he hadn't slept properly. The doctor at the health centre can help, and they can refer you to a counsellor." The next morning she went with him on the bus.

passage: In Copenhagen, Lars, twenty-one, had been struggling since autumn. He slept badly, missed seminars and had cancelled dinner with Noa three times. "It's just the dark months," he told her. She did, and he called from the café, voice unsteady. The appointment was for Thursday. He let out a long breath.

passage: I'm Kiran; Trisha and I share an office. I can't know everything she was thinking, but I watched how she handled getting help. First she checked every therapist's registration online and asked about their qualifications. She ignored an ad for a "life coach" promising quick fixes. After three sessions with the first psychologist she told me, "It's not clicking." I thought she'd give up. She didn't. She told the psychologist honestly, got a referral and tried another, and that one fit. Then one Sunday night she called me, sounding terrible. She said, "I've called the crisis line, and I'm going to the hospital. I didn't want to wait till Monday." I met her there. She's steadier now, and she's still going every week.

qa.a: She seems to feel more comfortable and steady, since she keeps going every week.

passage: "Noor, you asked how to find a good therapist. Let me tell you what I learnt the hard way. When I was twenty-four, I went first to a man who promised to cure my sadness in one week with herbs. Nothing changed, and I lost months. Then my sister found a licensed psychiatrist at the district hospital. After a month I stopped going; I felt better and thought I was done. Two months later I was worse. I went back and stayed the full course. And once, on a very bad night, I didn't wait for my appointment. I went to the hospital emergency. That's how I learnt: check the licence, give it time, find someone who fits, and in a crisis, go straight for help." Naveen smiled.
